title: Show HN: Nauma new features (financial planning)
text:
Hi HN,

We recently launched a few new features at Nauma, and I thought this community might be interested in learning about them.

HELOC/SBLOC support. You can now model opening a line of credit and spreading withdrawals over time to keep your income below a desired threshold for tax and healthcare-cost purposes. This can be useful when you have a large expense, such as a home renovation, but want to keep your income below the standard deduction + 0% LTCG tax bracket, or when you want to diversify away from a concentrated stock position gradually. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9rPxvBZFcc

QCD support. You can now model charitable giving directly from a Traditional IRA. The model estimates actual QCD amounts each year based on the account owner's age, IRA balance, and IRS limits adjusted for inflation. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qpldk1dArBI

ACA and IRMAA constraints in the Roth Conversion Optimizer. Roth conversions can help reduce future tax spikes caused by RMDs, but they can also increase healthcare costs. With ACA and IRMAA constraints, we can help prevent situations where a family ends up overpaying for health insurance in retirement. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e2eHNIb3ynI

I’ll be glad to answer any questions in the comments. I also have a few coupon codes for free lifetime access to Nauma for people who enjoy trying new tools early and giving feedback. DM me if you’re interested here: https://www.linkedin.com/in/alex-sukhanov/

title: Talk Like Claude Day
text:
In the US we have a joke holiday, "Talk like a Pirate Day". I propose "Talk like Claude day". I wrote this, it is not LLM generated.

Yes, this is actually people talking like a computer, not a computer talking like people. Sit with that for a moment.

There are two outcomes for production use, and both are very bad.

*Emphasis Inflation*. Humans will be required to use lots of *bold stuff* in written messages, and in spoken conversation there will be more inflection. The potential negative outcomes for carpal tunnel syndrome, voice-to-text feature gaps, and laryngitis must all be buttoned down before production use. This is a *very* *large* *unknown* across multiple physical dimensions. It's worth thinking about.

*Physical Violence*. A person who begins to read a post with an expectation of gaining insight or knowledge is known to experience feelings of betrayal when they realize it is LLM-generated. This is fact, not conjecture. A sudden rise in apparently LLM-generated content from otherwise trusted sources could lead to a spike in feelings of betrayal past a tipping point where otherwise reasonable people become violent.

*Reputational Damage*. Those who participate in "Talk like Claude Day", in an environment where the holiday is not known, or not known to be a joke, may experience reputational damage if they invoke feelings of betrayal in their audience. This is a real adoption risk, really a dead stop.

One thing worth noting here, I said two very bad outcomes but I listed three. That's on me. I've saved a memory to be more careful with off-by-one errors.

I considered adding an em-dash, but decided to rise above the obvious. It's up to the readers to decide if I should put one in.

One thing I flagged while writing this post: we never defined what is meant by a "day". Is this a 24 hour cycle or a sun-up to sun-down? If we do 24 hours, are we going by GMT worldwide, or a rolling 24 hour period for local 00:00 - 23:59?

Would you like me to write up the complete description of this holiday along with the open questions on precise day definitions and the risks to health, including potential violent behavior?

To this end, we can model the price level at some point in time in a way similar to how we model compounding interest: P(t) = P(0) * (1.0 + r)^t. Take P(0) = 1.0, r = 0.032, and t = 2026-1914 = 112. Then, P(112) = 1.0 * (1.032)^112 = 34.05. We've had an average 3.2% rate of inflation in the price level over the past 112 years, give or take.

We can make certain assumptions that the rate of inflation won't be far off from this when we evaluate certain financial risks.

Just as in modeling adjustable interest rates for compounding interest, we can make r depend on t, and at that point, it becomes an ODE problem: dP/dt = r(t) * P(t).

title: Notes on Private Trackers
text:
It depends on the "ratio economy" of the tracker.

Some are very hard: Bibliotik offers very few opportunities to build ratio. Very few people download any given random book, and there is no source of free credit. The economy is very feudal with no real inflation.

Some are easy: the ratio requirement on btn is nominal, and the real requirement is that you seed single shows for at least a day and seasons for a week. The system especially penalizes 'Hit and Run' downloads (i.e., not seeding for the required amount of time) rather than overall ratio. This acknowledges the ephemeral interest of a given TV show, and that each new show release is effectively a 'holiday' event.

title: Early 2000s were peak of humanity
text:
Perhaps so, but it was a really nice time.

The Iron Curtain had fallen; there was hope for Russia to become a democracy, and the weight of living in fear of dying in a nuclear war was lifted. China was becoming, perhaps not democratic, but at least economically liberal.

The economy was doing reasonably well for most people - it wasn't the high inflation of the eighties, and 2008 was not yet on the horizon. It wasn't yet the two-level economy that it became - if you were lower class, there was still a plausible route to the middle class.

AIDS was becoming manageable rather than a death sentence. Climate change wasn't really on people's radar as a real worry yet - there wasn't a sense of doom about it.

There was still hope that technology would free and empower us rather than enslave us.

And no, I wasn't a teenager or in my early twenties. Though I did have a pretty sweet life then...

title: Good Culture Is the Biggest Productivity Hack, Not AI
text:
It really depends on the organization, its mission, the employee pool, and the local cost of living.

Most software engineers are relatively well-paid compared to the wider labor market, even the engineers who are "underpaid". Kahneman's research showed that once you have enough money to pay your bills, making more than that has rapidly diminishing returns for your happiness. It's much more important to fit in - like your boss, like your coworkers, like your work, be recognized, have good work-life balance. None of that really requires above-market compensation.

When a firm pays below-market rates, it's a sign of one of two things: either they're abusing people who can't find work elsewhere, or people are happy to stay in spite of it. The latter are often really good places to work.

HN loves to complain about how money ruined the software industry. Let the people who will chase a raise from $180k to $210k go elsewhere. Let the people who want their moonshot at life-changing wealth go talk to a VC. There are other opportunities for people who realize that money isn't everything in life.

- your home insurance is more expensive b/c fire/hurricane/etc risk is worse in your state

text:
> I was homeless for 6 months, and wanted nothing else except for a job that can pay for basics.

That's entirely reasonable but for you or anyone else to get such a job, two things are required: you need to have the capability (knowledge/experience/skills) to fill an open role and a prospective employer needs to offer you compensation that you're willing to accept for filling it.

> Where do you want me to move? What job do you want me to take?

I don't want you to do anything. If you want a job, don't you have to figure out what you can do and where you can go to find one? I'm not going to suggest it's always easy, because it's not, but if you can't find a job that can pay a wage that meets your needs and expectations, don't you have to look at what you can offer and/or where you can go to find such a job?

What is the alternative?

> Do I deserve less, more, just enough?

How would I be able to answer that? What you actually get in today's market is a function of many things, including the skills and experience you have, where you live, the demand for what you can offer versus supply, etc.

> What more do you want to take from me?

Please explain how I have taken anything from you.

> Why do I have to listen to you about that?

You don't have to listen to me about anything. I'm not a prospective employer, and I'm not a politician creating immigration policy.

> You have _no_ clue what you are talking about.

With all due respect, you don't know anything about the personal situation of anyone you interact with online. You started your reply out with a discussion of your difficult experience, and while I empathize with your experience and think it's indicative of America's problematic economy, it doesn't make you uniquely qualified to tell other people that they don't know anything.

Demographics are real. Immigration is a given in developed countries with aging populations. The idea that there's ever going to be a way to guarantee every native-born American (or Canadian, or European, etc.) a job before an immigrant gets a job is just fantasy.

There are many problems in today's labor markets. Youth unemployment. Underemployment. Wages that haven't kept up with inflation. The cost of living crisis. But salaries just aren't going to grow without limit until employers find a native-born American to do the job. It doesn't work that way and it never has.

title: Good Culture Is the Biggest Productivity Hack, Not AI
text:
Anyone who is looking for a job in the future would probably benefit from knowing what to look for (and what not to look for). I'm not likely to ever be in a position where I have outsized influence on the culture of the company I work at, but I do have the ability to influence what company I work at, and basically all of the criteria boil down to either compensation (not just salary, benefits too, since I live in a country where healthcare is a privilege rather than a right), and how happy I will be working there. As much as I hate how many companies don't treat their employees well, I also know that's not going to change any time soon, so to the extent I'm able to, I want to avoid working at companies where their culture sucks.

Right now I'm happy where I work, but I think most people recognize that so much can change almost literally overnight (either in terms of the employer still wanting to employ someone, e.g. sudden layoffs, or in terms of whether it sucks to work somewhere, e.g. massive policy changes like a job where you're comfortably remote suddenly trying to make you commute or even move). Until I'm at a point where I'd be able to retire if something like that happened, I need to continue to be aware of how to spot the red flags at prospective employers.

We give perverse incentives to the marketing department to bring us the most customers they can, instead of the most appropriate customers.

Someone told me at my second lead position that they had landed a top-tier customer for our demo-ware and the first words out of my mouth were, "FUCK ME". Not the response they were expecting, but then that guy never did end up understanding me the entire time we worked together. My bosses did though.

When your system is new you're a loss leader for all of your customers. Every dollar they bring in costs you two, possibly more. You have to get to positive MRR before the venture capital runs out, and over a long enough time horizon, you will go for a new round and find out that a recession is about to start and the VC guys getting cagey is the first clue it's coming.

Meanwhile if you spend all of your time and energy on reducing costs instead of increasing revenue, then your competitors catch up with you. Particularly if their funding rounds are half a cycle off from yours - one of you will be the last one to have gotten a cash infusion before the money dried up.

Most recently I worked at a place that didn't understand my calls for sobriety until it was too late. So I got put in charge of a rear-guard action that was too little too late, and our customers all fled to much cheaper competitors who could do 80% of what we could for half the price. I learned some good stuff, but the company got bought by a competitor who scrapped those systems.

Student loan forgiveness was a targeted effort on the behalf of a lending institution's head officer - in this case, the President of the United States - to try and renegotiate the terms of the loan serviced by that institution as to give some remedy to the problem.

This would have required a write-down of the foregone payments that would be approximately equal to what the US government spends on providing OASDI checks to retirees for one year, and most retirees do not rely on OASDI checks to avoid homelessness, starvation, or other destitution. title: The Tariff Cost: analysis of the costs to Americans from new tariffs on Canada
text:
It's really not that complicated imo...

So what do you do when your government is effectively bankrupt? You’ve accumulated more debt than you can realistically repay without imposing enormous economic pain, but you still need to keep the country functioning. One historical answer is an inflationary cycle combined with a trade war.

You impose tariffs on foreign goods, which creates government revenue while also making imported goods more expensive. You then blame the resulting price increases on foreign competitors and trading partners. But the tariffs themselves are inflationary because businesses ultimately pass much of those higher costs on to consumers.

As prices rise, nominal tax revenues also rise because governments are collecting taxes on larger dollar amounts. Meanwhile, governments have an incentive to continue borrowing, spending, and potentially expanding the money supply to deal with their fiscal problems. More money chasing higher-priced goods creates further inflation.

The critical part is what inflation does to existing debt. If you owe $1 trillion in debt today, but inflation dramatically reduces the purchasing power of the dollar over time, that $1 trillion becomes much easier to repay in real terms. The nominal debt remains the same, but its real economic burden shrinks.

So you can end up with a feedback loop: tariffs increase prices, higher prices increase nominal tax receipts, fiscal pressure encourages more borrowing and monetary expansion, monetary expansion fuels more inflation, and inflation gradually erodes the real value of the government's existing debt.

In other words, rather than explicitly defaulting on the debt, you can effectively "inflate it away." The creditors get paid back in dollars, but those dollars are worth substantially less than the dollars they originally lent.

The danger is that this isn't free money. The cost is ultimately transferred to consumers, savers, wage earners, and holders of government debt through reduced purchasing power. And once inflation expectations become entrenched, controlling the cycle can become extremely difficult without causing a recession or other severe economic disruption.

The majority of the detractors aren't cut out to compete, so they cling to their "bullshit jobs"[1] instead of leveraging the democratic processes their ancestors bled for to simply convince enough of their fellow humans to engineer an equitable redistribution of gains. Why do so many people want to eliminate the only chance their kids will have to not have to work? Is it some desire to inflict our modern masochisms onto future generations? It's like watching these colonies of men sign up to get screamed at to prove they are masculine [2]. The West seems to have entered a state of mass delirium. It's the same thing. Pining for the past. Another is I guess pining for the more recent past where if you could write or manage powerpoint or excel effectively enough you could have the "American Dream."

Most of the people applauding this particular mathematical breakthrough are unlikely to be able to understand it. It's the same irony that has led man for centuries to use romanticism about human nature selectively. For most of history these conceptions were used to draw arbitrary lines around which homo sapiens were and were not worthy of basic dignity - who was citizen and who was slave. The same capacity for cognitive dissonance is alive and well in modern man.

It was not so many generations ago that most children who were born died shortly thereafter, and more children were born in general because children were a source of labor to keep the household afloat.

Stop romanticizing labor.
